options.A: To break the chain of infection
options.B: To accelerate wound healing
options.C: To reduce hospital utility bills
options.D: To test new laboratory equipment

explanation: Isolation aims to break the chain of infection, protecting patients, staff, and visitors from acquiring secondary infections. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T4#GNS313_U2_T4_h2)

question: When should isolation protocols ideally be implemented for a patient with suspected infectious disease?

options.A: Only after the patient is discharged
options.B: After laboratory confirmation is fully received
options.C: Immediately upon clinical suspicion
options.D: When the patient requests a private room

explanation: Isolation should be initiated promptly upon clinical suspicion rather than waiting for laboratory confirmation to prevent ongoing transmission. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T4#GNS313_U2_T4_h2)

question: Which type of precaution is required for pathogens transmitted through large respiratory droplets traveling short distances?

options.A: Contact precautions
options.B: Droplet precautions
options.C: Airborne precautions
options.D: Reverse precautions

explanation: Droplet precautions are specifically designed for pathogens spread via large respiratory droplets generated by coughing, sneezing, or talking. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T4#GNS313_U2_T4_h3)

question: Pulmonary tuberculosis requires which category of transmission-based precautions?

options.A: Contact precautions
options.B: Standard precautions only
options.C: Airborne precautions
options.D: Enteric precautions

explanation: Pulmonary tuberculosis spreads via small droplet nuclei that remain suspended in the air, necessitating airborne precautions and specialized ventilation. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T4#GNS313_U2_T4_h3)

question: To which group of patients should standard precautions be applied?

options.A: Only patients with confirmed infectious diseases
options.B: All patients regardless of their infection status
options.C: Only patients admitted to private isolation rooms
options.D: Only surgical patients undergoing major operations

explanation: Standard precautions are foundational practices applied universally to the care of all patients in all healthcare settings. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T4#GNS313_U2_T4_h4)

question: What distinguishes transmission-based precautions from standard precautions?

options.A: They replace hand hygiene entirely
options.B: They are only used in community health outreaches
options.C: They provide additional controls for highly transmissible pathogens
options.D: They are optional guidelines for nursing students

explanation: Transmission-based precautions provide extra barriers and controls specifically tailored for patients with suspected or confirmed transmissible pathogens. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T4#GNS313_U2_T4_h4)

question: When should personal protective equipment (PPE) typically be put on (donned)?

options.A: After leaving the patient's isolation room
options.B: Before entering the patient's room
options.C: Only when performing surgical procedures
options.D: During the debriefing session after shift change

explanation: PPE must be donned before entering the isolation room to ensure full barrier protection prior to any potential exposure. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T4#GNS313_U2_T4_h5)

question: Why is the correct sequence for doffing (taking off) PPE vital?

options.A: To speed up the nurse's tea break
options.B: To prevent self-contamination of the skin and clothing
options.C: To keep the gowns clean for laundry washing
options.D: To comply with hospital fashion codes

explanation: Following a precise doffing sequence prevents infectious agents on used PPE from transferring to the nurse's skin, mucous membranes, or scrubs. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T4#GNS313_U2_T4_h5)

question: What type of air pressure is maintained in an Airborne Infection Isolation Room (AIIR) to prevent pathogen escape?

options.A: Negative pressure
options.B: Positive pressure
options.C: Neutral pressure
options.D: Variable atmospheric pressure

explanation: Negative pressure ensures that air flows into the room when doors are opened, trapping airborne pathogens inside rather than releasing them into hallways. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T4#GNS313_U2_T4_h6)

question: How can nurses manage ventilation in resource-limited settings where mechanical negative pressure rooms are absent?

options.A: Seal all windows tightly and turn off fans
options.B: Utilize natural cross-ventilation by opening windows
options.C: Spray heavy perfumes in the corridors
options.D: Transfer all patients to the hospital lobby

explanation: In resource-constrained environments, natural cross-ventilation through open windows helps dilute and disperse airborne contaminants. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T4#GNS313_U2_T4_h6)

question: What is a common psychological effect experienced by patients placed in strict isolation?

options.A: Euphoria and excitement
options.B: Loneliness and anxiety
options.C: Complete emotional numbness
options.D: Enhanced physical strength

explanation: Physical separation and lack of social interaction frequently lead to feelings of loneliness, anxiety, and depression in isolated patients. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T4#GNS313_U2_T4_h7)

question: How can nurses best support the psychosocial well-being of an isolated patient?

options.A: Limit communication to absolute medical necessities only
options.B: Provide compassionate communication and facilitate alternative connections
options.C: Discourage visits or calls from family members permanently
options.D: Ignore emotional complaints since infection control is the only priority

explanation: Nurses support mental well-being by communicating empathetically, offering reassurance, and helping patients connect with loved ones safely. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T4#GNS313_U2_T4_h7)

question: What is a key responsibility of the community health nurse when an infectious patient is discharged home?

options.A: Isolate the entire community immediately
options.B: Establish home isolation protocols and educate family caregivers
options.C: Destroy all personal belongings of the patient
options.D: Prohibit any future medical follow-ups

explanation: Community health nurses educate families on safe home isolation, hygiene, and waste disposal to ensure safe continuity of care. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T4#GNS313_U2_T4_h8)

question: How do community health nurses contribute during a disease outbreak in a rural Nigerian setting?

options.A: By closing down all local markets permanently
options.B: By conducting active surveillance and contact tracing
options.C: By ignoring local health practices
options.D: By treating patients exclusively without recording data

explanation: Active surveillance and contact tracing are essential community health nursing functions used to track and contain disease outbreaks at the grassroots level. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T4#GNS313_U2_T4_h8)

question: What is the primary purpose of quarantine in public health?

options.A: To treat patients who are actively showing severe symptoms of an infection
options.B: To restrict movement of individuals potentially exposed to a disease during its incubation period
options.C: To permanently relocate individuals from endemic rural zones to urban hospitals
options.D: To punish individuals who refuse to take routine vaccinations

explanation: Quarantine restricts the movement of individuals who have been exposed to a contagious disease but are not yet showing symptoms, allowing observation during the incubation period. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T5#GNS313_U2_T5_h1)

question: Which of the following diseases mentioned is a relevant context for quarantine protocols in Nigeria?

options.A: Essential hypertension
options.B: Iron deficiency anemia
options.C: Lassa fever
options.D: Osteoarthritis

explanation: Lassa fever is a viral hemorrhagic fever prevalent in the region that often necessitates strict public health interventions like quarantine and infection control. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T5#GNS313_U2_T5_h1)

question: Who is the target population for quarantine, distinguishing it from isolation?

options.A: Asymptomatic individuals with potential exposure to a contagious disease
options.B: Patients who have tested positive and are actively symptomatic
options.C: Healthcare workers who have completed their shift in an emergency ward
options.D: Healthy members of the general public with no history of contact

question: What is a negative consequence of failing to provide clear public health education during a quarantine response?

question: Which of the following best describes a primary role of the community health nurse in quarantine management?

question: What is defined as an organism or substance in which an infectious agent normally lives, multiplies, and depends on for survival?

question: According to the text, why is understanding non-human reservoirs particularly important in tropical regions like Nigeria?

question: What is the primary purpose of reservoir destruction in public health practice?

options.C: Within 14 days

explanation: HIV PEP is highly time-sensitive and should ideally be started within 2 hours of exposure, and not later than 72 hours, for a 28-day course. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T8#GNS313_U2_T8_h7)

question: What is a primary challenge community health nurses often face in Nigerian primary healthcare centers?

options.C: Zero community participation
options.D: Excessive funding that is difficult to allocate

explanation: Primary health care centers in Nigeria frequently face infrastructural challenges like a lack of running water and electricity, requiring resourceful community nursing strategies. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T8#GNS313_U2_T8_h8)

question: How do community health nurses promote infection control compliance among local healthcare workers and traditional birth attendants?

options.A: By shutting down clinics that do not meet international tertiary standards
options.B: Through participatory education, training, and implementing context-appropriate safety practices
options.C: By forbidding anyone without a university degree from providing care
options.D: By relying solely on written policy manuals sent via mail

explanation: Community health nurses use participatory education and context-appropriate methods to train local workers and traditional birth attendants in safe practices. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T8#GNS313_U2_T8_h8)

question: Which of the following hepatitis viruses is primarily transmitted via the fecal-oral route?

options.A: Hepatitis B
options.B: Hepatitis C
options.C: Hepatitis A
options.D: Hepatitis D

explanation: Hepatitis A virus is typically transmitted via the fecal-oral route, commonly through contaminated food and water. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T16#GNS313_U2_T16_h1)

question: Why is Hepatitis D unique in its ability to cause infection?

options.A: It is transmitted exclusively through contaminated water.
options.B: It is a defective virus that requires an active Hepatitis B infection to replicate.
options.C: It only causes acute, self-limiting infections without complications.
options.D: It belongs to a family of DNA viruses that affect the kidneys.

explanation: Hepatitis D is a defective RNA virus that can only replicate in the presence of an active Hepatitis B infection. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T16#GNS313_U2_T16_h1)

question: What is the primary mechanism of hepatocyte injury in viral hepatitis?

options.A: Direct toxic action of bacterial endotoxins
options.B: Cell-mediated immune response attacking infected liver cells
options.C: Obstruction of the bile ducts by gallstones
options.D: Ischemia caused by systemic hypotension

explanation: Hepatocyte injury is primarily caused by the body's cell-mediated immune response, where cytotoxic T lymphocytes attack the virus-infected liver cells. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T16#GNS313_U2_T16_h2)

question: Impaired synthesis of clotting factors in the liver directly places the client at risk for which complication?

options.A: Hyperglycemia
options.B: Prolonged bleeding and hemorrhage
options.C: Severe dehydration
options.D: Hypertension

explanation: When the liver fails to synthesize vital clotting factors like prothrombin, the client experiences prolonged bleeding times and an increased risk of hemorrhage. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T16#GNS313_U2_T16_h2)

question: Which of the following describes the primary mode of transmission for Hepatitis A and E?

options.A: Parenteral exposure to infected blood
options.B: Fecal-oral route via contaminated food or water
options.C: Airborne droplets from coughing and sneezing
options.D: Vector-borne transmission through mosquito bites

explanation: Hepatitis A and E are primarily spread through the fecal-oral route, often via contaminated food and water supplies in areas with poor sanitation. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T16#GNS313_U2_T16_h3)

question: Which of the following is a major risk factor for transmitting Hepatitis B, C, and D?

options.A: Drinking unboiled water
options.B: Eating improperly cooked shellfish
options.C: Exposure to infected blood through unsafe injections or needle-sticks
options.D: Living in overcrowded housing with poor ventilation

explanation: Hepatitis B, C, and D are bloodborne pathogens transmitted through percutaneous or mucosal contact with infected blood, such as through unsafe injections or needle-sticks. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T16#GNS313_U2_T16_h3)

question: During which phase of acute viral hepatitis does the client typically develop jaundice, dark urine, and clay-colored stools?

options.A: Pre-icteric phase
options.B: Icteric phase
options.C: Post-icteric phase
options.D: Asymptomatic chronic phase

explanation: The icteric phase is characterized by the appearance of jaundice, dark urine, and clay-colored stools due to hyperbilirubinemia. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T16#GNS313_U2_T16_h4)

question: What is a key clinical characteristic of chronic Hepatitis B and C infections?

options.A: They always present with sudden, severe acute liver failure within 48 hours.
options.B: They are frequently asymptomatic for years until advanced complications develop.
options.C: They are characterized by persistent diarrhea and rapid weight gain.
options.D: They resolve spontaneously without any long-term health consequences.

explanation: Chronic infections are often insidious and remain asymptomatic for years, frequently leading to late presentation when advanced liver disease occurs. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T16#GNS313_U2_T16_h4)

question: Which serological marker indicates an active, ongoing Hepatitis B infection?

options.A: Anti-HBs
options.B: HBsAg
options.C: Anti-HAV IgG
options.D: Anti-HCV

explanation: Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) is the primary marker used to indicate an active, ongoing Hepatitis B infection. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T16#GNS313_U2_T16_h5)

question: What do elevated serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) levels primarily indicate?

options.A: Renal function impairment
options.B: Hepatocellular injury and inflammation
options.C: Enhanced liver protein synthesis
options.D: Normal biliary excretion

explanation: Elevated serum ALT and AST levels are primary indicators of hepatocellular injury and active inflammation in the liver. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T16#GNS313_U2_T16_h5)

question: What is the primary treatment approach for acute, uncomplicated Hepatitis A infection?

options.A: Long-term direct-acting antiviral therapy
options.B: Supportive care including rest, hydration, and avoiding hepatotoxic substances
options.C: Immediate orthotopic liver transplantation
options.D: High-dose corticosteroid administration

explanation: Acute uncomplicated Hepatitis A is managed with supportive care, including rest, hydration, and avoiding substances that stress the liver like alcohol. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T16#GNS313_U2_T16_h6)

question: Which class of medications has revolutionized the treatment of chronic Hepatitis C, achieving high cure rates?

options.A: Direct-acting antivirals (DAAs)
options.B: Broad-spectrum antibiotics
options.C: Loop diuretics
options.D: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs

explanation: Direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) are highly effective medications that achieve high cure rates for chronic Hepatitis C. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T16#GNS313_U2_T16_h6)

question: What is an important dietary recommendation for a client experiencing acute viral hepatitis with nausea and anorexia?

options.A: Three large, high-fat meals per day
options.B: Small, frequent meals tailored to tolerance
options.C: Strict fasting for 48 hours
options.D: High-protein, low-carbohydrate diet

explanation: Small, frequent meals help manage nausea and ensure adequate nutritional intake for clients experiencing anorexia during acute hepatitis. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T16#GNS313_U2_T16_h7)

question: Which of the following substances should clients with viral hepatitis be strictly instructed to avoid?

options.A: Plain water
options.B: Alcohol and hepatotoxic medications
options.C: Fresh fruits and vegetables
options.D: Oral rehydration salts

explanation: Clients must strictly avoid alcohol and hepatotoxic substances (like paracetamol) to prevent further stress and injury to the liver. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T16#GNS313_U2_T16_h7)

question: When is the first dose of the Hepatitis B vaccine ideally administered to infants under immunization programs?

options.A: At adolescence before puberty

options.C: At five years of age upon entering primary school
options.D: Only if the mother tests negative for HBsAg

explanation: The Hepatitis B vaccine is recommended as a birth dose within the first 24 hours of life to effectively prevent vertical and early childhood transmission. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T16#GNS313_U2_T16_h8)

question: What intervention is indicated for a non-immune healthcare worker who experiences an accidental needle-stick injury from an HBsAg-positive patient?

options.A: Administration of Hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) and the Hepatitis B vaccine
options.B: A single dose of oral paracetamol and bed rest
options.C: Immediate liver biopsy and antiviral therapy
options.D: Prophylactic antibiotics for ten days

explanation: Post-exposure prophylaxis for Hepatitis B exposure in non-immune individuals involves administering both HBIG and the Hepatitis B vaccine. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T16#GNS313_U2_T16_h8)

question: What is the primary role of adequate nutrition in public health according to the text?

options.A: Acting as a foundational shield against acute and chronic diseases
options.B: Replacing the need for all pharmacotherapy in hospitals
options.C: Eliminating the need for primary healthcare centers
options.D: Reversing genetic mutations completely

explanation: Adequate nutrition serves as a foundational shield against a multitude of acute and chronic diseases, supporting physiological resilience. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T13#GNS313_U2_T13_h1)

question: Why is nutritional advocacy particularly important for public health nurses in Nigeria?

options.A: Because dietary practices have no impact on non-communicable diseases
options.B: To address food security, socioeconomic barriers, and reduce hospital admissions
options.C: To completely eliminate the prevalence of malaria through diet alone
options.D: Because Nigeria has no infrastructural challenges in healthcare

explanation: Nurses must address food security and socioeconomic barriers to reduce hospital admissions and foster a healthier workforce. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T13#GNS313_U2_T13_h1)

question: What occurs to the immune system during states of severe nutritional deficiency?

options.A: It becomes hypersensitive and attacks all body tissues
options.B: It experiences impaired phagocytosis and reduced antibody production
options.C: It permanently increases its production of T-cells
options.D: It remains entirely unaffected by dietary intake

explanation: Nutritional deficiencies lead to a breakdown in immunity, characterized by impaired phagocytosis and reduced antibody production. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T13#GNS313_U2_T13_h2)

question: What is a direct immunological consequence of protein-energy malnutrition mentioned in the text?

options.A: Thymic atrophy and compromised cell-mediated immunity
options.B: Hypertrophy of the spleen and elevated white blood cell counts
options.C: Enhanced mucosal integrity in the respiratory tract
options.D: Immediate resistance to all bacterial pathogens

explanation: Protein-energy malnutrition directly leads to thymic atrophy, which severely compromises cell-mediated immunity. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T13#GNS313_U2_T13_h2)

question: What is the primary role of high-quality proteins in disease defense?

options.A: Acting as primary antioxidants against free radicals
options.B: Supplying amino acids for immunoglobulins and enzymes
options.C: Maintaining mucosal epithelial tissues exclusively
options.D: Serving as cofactors for iron transport

explanation: High-quality proteins supply the essential amino acids required to form immunoglobulins, enzymes, and other immune-related molecules. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T13#GNS313_U2_T13_h3)

question: Which micronutrient is specifically highlighted for maintaining the integrity of mucosal epithelial tissues?

options.A: Vitamin A
options.B: Iron
options.C: Selenium
options.D: Zinc

explanation: Vitamin A is vital in public health for maintaining the integrity of mucosal epithelial tissues, forming the first line of defense. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T13#GNS313_U2_T13_h3)

question: How do communicable infections affect an individual's nutritional status?

options.A: They improve nutrient absorption in the gut
options.B: They have no impact on metabolic demands
options.C: They worsen nutritional status through increased metabolic demands and nutrient loss
options.D: They instantly boost the body's protein reserves

explanation: Infections worsen nutritional status due to increased metabolic demands, nutrient loss, and decreased appetite (anorexia). [learn more](GNS313_U2_T13#GNS313_U2_T13_h4)

question: What is a common consequence of measles when it occurs in a malnourished child compared to a well-nourished one?

options.A: It remains entirely asymptomatic
options.B: It frequently results in severe complications like pneumonia and death
options.C: It causes immediate immunity to all other viral diseases
options.D: It prevents future episodes of malnutrition

explanation: In a malnourished child, measles frequently results in severe, life-threatening complications such as pneumonia, diarrhea, and death. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T13#GNS313_U2_T13_h4)

question: What is an advantage of public health interventions like food fortification?

options.A: It requires individuals to completely change their daily shopping habits
options.B: It ensures entire populations receive essential micronutrients without individual behavioral changes
options.C: It completely replaces the need for community education workshops
options.D: It focuses solely on treating severe cases inside tertiary hospitals

explanation: Food fortification delivers essential micronutrients broadly to populations without necessitating individual behavioral modifications. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T13#GNS313_U2_T13_h5)

question: What is the primary objective of Community-Based Management of Acute Malnutrition (CMAM) programs?

options.A: To identify and treat acute malnutrition early before hospitalization is needed
options.B: To supply high-cost pharmaceuticals to urban hospitals
options.C: To discourage exclusive breastfeeding in rural communities
options.D: To replace traditional agriculture with imported food items

explanation: CMAM programs empower local workers to identify and treat acute malnutrition early, preventing severe complications. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T13#GNS313_U2_T13_h5)

question: Which anthropometric measurement is commonly used by nurses in community outreach to rapidly screen for malnutrition in children?

options.A: Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC)
options.B: Blood glucose level
options.C: Serum electrolyte concentration
options.D: Basal metabolic rate

question: Why is specialized nutritional assessment particularly important for pregnant and lactating women?

options.A: To prevent low birth weight and maternal mortality
options.B: Because they are immune to all communicable diseases
options.C: To eliminate the need for antenatal clinic visits
options.D: Because their metabolic demands remain completely constant

explanation: Assessing and monitoring pregnant and lactating women helps prevent complications like low birth weight and maternal mortality. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T13#GNS313_U2_T13_h6)

question: What is an effective approach for nurses when educating Nigerian mothers on weaning foods?

options.A: Recommending only expensive imported food formulas

options.C: Discouraging the use of any local agricultural products

question: How do nurses extend their impact beyond individual patient care regarding nutrition in communities?

options.A: By collaborating with community leaders and advocating for supportive policies like workplace breastfeeding guidelines
options.B: By focusing exclusively on inpatient surgical interventions
options.C: By ignoring cultural food practices and imposing foreign diets
options.D: By working entirely in isolation from other healthcare sectors

explanation: Nurses amplify their impact by collaborating with community stakeholders and advocating for policies like workplace breastfeeding guidelines. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T13#GNS313_U2_T13_h7)

question: Which of the following best describes the clinical onset of enteric fevers?

options.A: Sudden onset of high spiking fever and relative tachycardia

options.C: Rapid onset of localized skin rashes and joint pain

question: Which demographic group bears the disproportionate burden of enteric fever infections?

options.A: Neonates and infants under one year
options.B: School-aged children and young adults
options.C: Elderly individuals over the age of sixty-five
options.D: Middle-aged adults with occupational hand injuries

explanation: The disease burden of enteric fevers falls disproportionately on school-aged children and young adults, particularly in regions with suboptimal sanitation. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T17#GNS313_U2_T17_h1)

question: What is the primary natural reservoir for Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi?

options.A: Domestic pigs and cattle
options.B: Contaminated soil and stagnant ponds
options.C: Human beings
options.D: Wild rodents and vectors like mosquitoes

explanation: Humans serve as the only natural reservoir and definitive host for Salmonella Typhi and Paratyphi organisms. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T17#GNS313_U2_T17_h2)

question: Through which primary route do enteric fevers transmit between individuals?

options.A: Direct aerosol inhalation
options.B: Fecal-oral route
options.C: Vector-borne tick bites
options.D: Transplacental maternal transfer

question: Which intestinal structures are specifically targeted by Salmonella bacteria during initial invasion?

options.A: Brunner's glands in the duodenum
options.B: Peyer's patches in the terminal ileum
options.C: Crypts of Lieberkühn in the jejunum
options.D: Villi in the proximal duodenum

question: What are 'rose spots', sometimes observed during the second week of enteric fever?

options.A: Necrotic ulcers on the oral mucosa

options.C: Faint, blanching erythematous macules on the trunk
options.D: Painful subcutaneous nodules on the lower extremities

explanation: Rose spots are faint, blanching erythematous macules that typically appear on the trunk during the second week of illness. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T17#GNS313_U2_T17_h3)

question: Which diagnostic test is considered the gold standard during the first week of enteric fever?

options.A: Widal serological test
options.B: Blood culture
options.C: Complete blood count
options.D: Stool microscopy

explanation: Blood culture is the gold standard for diagnosing enteric fever, showing the highest sensitivity during the first week of illness when bacteremia is peak. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T17#GNS313_U2_T17_h4)

question: What hematological finding is most commonly associated with uncomplicated enteric fever?

options.A: Leukopenia with relative neutropenia
options.B: Marked leukocytosis with a left shift
options.C: Trombocytosis with elevated clotting times
options.D: Polycythemia vera secondary to dehydration

explanation: Uncomplicated enteric fever typically presents with leukopenia and relative neutropenia on a complete blood count. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T17#GNS313_U2_T17_h4)

question: Which class of antibiotics includes agents commonly used to treat enteric fevers based on sensitivity patterns?

options.A: First-generation penicillins

options.C: Aminoglycosides
options.D: Sulfonamides alone

explanation: Third-generation cephalosporins, such as ceftriaxone, are commonly used for treating enteric fevers, especially in areas with widespread antimicrobial resistance. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T17#GNS313_U2_T17_h5)

question: What type of diet is generally recommended for a patient with enteric fever recovering in the hospital?

options.A: High-fiber, roughage-rich diet
options.B: Soft, low-residue diet
options.C: High-protein, raw vegetable diet
options.D: Strict high-fat ketogenic diet

explanation: A soft, low-residue diet is recommended to minimize mechanical irritation and stress on ulcerated Peyer's patches in the small intestine. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T17#GNS313_U2_T17_h5)

question: During which week of illness do severe complications such as intestinal hemorrhage and perforation typically manifest?

options.A: First week
options.B: Second week
options.C: Third week
options.D: Fifth week

explanation: Severe complications such as intestinal hemorrhage and perforation typically arise during the third week of untreated or delayed enteric fever. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T17#GNS313_U2_T17_h6)

question: What are the hallmark clinical signs of an intestinal perforation in a patient with enteric fever?

options.A: Sudden severe abdominal pain, rigidity, and rebound tenderness
options.B: High spiking fever and generalized maculopapular rash
options.C: Severe productive cough with blood-tinged sputum
options.D: Marked peripheral edema and hypertension

explanation: Intestinal perforation causes sudden, severe abdominal pain, abdominal rigidity, rebound tenderness, and clinical signs of peritonitis. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T17#GNS313_U2_T17_h6)

question: What is considered a primary structural intervention required to control enteric fevers at a community level?

options.C: Widespread administration of prophylactic antimalarials
options.D: Daily administration of topical antiseptic washes

explanation: Providing safe, potable drinking water and reliable sewage disposal systems are primary structural interventions needed to prevent waterborne enteric fevers. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T17#GNS313_U2_T17_h7)

question: Why is the identification and treatment of chronic carriers important in public health control?

options.C: It stops the transmission of airborne droplet nuclei
options.D: It guarantees permanent immunity for the entire community

question: What is the primary definition of food poisoning in a clinical context?

question: Which group of individuals is at the highest risk for severe complications from food poisoning?

options.A: Young, healthy adult males
options.B: Infants, pregnant women, and the elderly
options.C: Professional athletes in training
options.D: Individuals with high physical endurance

explanation: Vulnerable populations such as infants, pregnant women, the elderly, and immunocompromised individuals are at the highest risk for severe complications. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T19#GNS313_U2_T19_h1)

question: Which category of pathogens is the leading cause of infectious foodborne illnesses in Nigeria?

options.A: Fungi
options.B: Bacteria
options.C: Prions
options.D: Helminths

explanation: Bacterial pathogens are the leading cause of infectious foodborne illnesses in Nigeria, heavily driven by warm tropical temperatures. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T19#GNS313_U2_T19_h2)

question: How is Staphylococcus aureus typically introduced into ready-to-eat foods like pastries and salads?

options.A: Through contaminated irrigation water used on fields
options.B: Through infected food handlers touching the food
options.C: Via airborne transmission in cold storage units
options.D: From improper chemical fertilizer application

question: What characterizes food intoxication compared to food infection?

options.A: It involves the ingestion of pre-formed bacterial toxins already present in the food.
options.B: It requires a long incubation period of several weeks for microbes to multiply.
options.C: It is exclusively caused by viral pathogens attacking the respiratory tract.
options.D: It prevents any fluid loss from the intestinal lumen.

explanation: Food intoxication involves ingesting pre-formed bacterial toxins that act rapidly without needing active microbial proliferation inside the host. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T19#GNS313_U2_T19_h3)

question: What is the primary mode of transmission for most foodborne pathogens?

options.A: Direct airborne droplet inhalation
options.B: Vector-borne transmission via mosquitoes
options.C: Fecal-oral route through poor hygiene and contaminated water
options.D: Transplacental transmission from mother to foetus

explanation: Modes of transmission are predominantly fecal-oral, facilitated by poor personal hygiene, contaminated water, and improper food handling. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T19#GNS313_U2_T19_h3)

question: What are the classic acute gastrointestinal symptoms of food poisoning?

options.A: Constipation and weight gain
options.B: Nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, and diarrhea
options.C: Chronic heartburn and acid reflux
options.D: Jaundice and upper right quadrant pain

question: Which clinical presentation is specifically associated with neurotoxic food poisoning like botulism?

options.D: Localized skin rashes and intense pruritus

question: What is a crucial component of the initial health history for a patient with suspected food poisoning?

options.A: Family history of cardiovascular disease
options.B: Recent dietary intake and whether others sharing the meal are ill
options.C: Childhood vaccination records
options.D: Occupational history of chemical exposure over the last decade

question: Which blood tests are essential for assessing electrolyte and fluid balance complications in food poisoning?

options.B: Serum electrolyte panels and renal function tests
options.C: Coagulation profile and blood typing
options.D: Thyroid stimulating hormone test

question: What is the cornerstone treatment and primary nursing objective for managing food poisoning?

options.A: Immediate administration of broad-spectrum prophylactic antibiotics
options.B: Prevention and correction of dehydration and electrolyte imbalances
options.C: Surgical resection of the inflamed bowel segment
options.D: Complete dietary restriction and total parenteral nutrition

question: Why are anti-motility drugs often avoided in cases of invasive bacterial food poisoning?

options.A: They cause permanent paralysis of the skeletal muscles.

options.C: They instantly induce severe hypertension.
options.D: They neutralize the effectiveness of oral rehydration salts.

question: What is Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS), a severe complication of certain bacterial food poisonings, characterized by?

question: Which bacterial pathogen is strongly associated with the subsequent development of Guillain-Barré syndrome?

options.D: Salmonella typhi

question: What is one of the core principles included in the World Health Organization's 'Five Keys to Safer Food' promoted by nurses?

options.C: Storing all perishable food items at room temperature
options.D: Reusing cooking water multiple times for economic efficiency

explanation: A key safety principle is separating raw and cooked food to prevent cross-contamination of pathogens. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T19#GNS313_U2_T19_h8)

question: Why is leaving cooked meals at ambient tropical temperatures for extended periods dangerous?

options.A: It causes the food to lose its color completely.
options.B: It accelerates rapid bacterial proliferation due to the warm climate.
options.C: It attracts harmless environmental insects.
options.D: It freezes the moisture inside the food matrix.

explanation: Warm tropical temperatures accelerate microbial multiplication and bacterial proliferation in food left out too long. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T19#GNS313_U2_T19_h8)

question: What are the primary anatomical structures inflamed in gastroenteritis?

options.A: The esophagus and stomach
options.B: The stomach and small intestines
options.C: The large intestine and rectum
options.D: The liver and pancreas

explanation: Gastroenteritis is defined as the inflammation of the mucous membrane of both the stomach and the small intestines. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T20#GNS313_U2_T20_h1)

question: Which of the following is a classic clinical presentation of acute gastroenteritis?

options.A: Constipation and high fever
options.B: Watery diarrhea and vomiting
options.C: Bloody sputum and chest pain
options.D: Jaundice and right upper quadrant pain

explanation: Acute gastroenteritis is classically characterized by an acute onset of watery diarrhea, often accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and abdominal cramps. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T20#GNS313_U2_T20_h1)

question: Which pathogen is recognized as the leading cause of severe acute gastroenteritis in infants and young children in Nigeria?

options.A: Vibrio cholerae
options.B: Rotavirus
options.C: Giardia lamblia
options.D: Salmonella typhi

explanation: Rotavirus is well-documented as the leading viral cause of severe acute gastroenteritis in infants and young children globally and in Nigeria. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T20#GNS313_U2_T20_h2)

question: Through which primary route are most gastroenteritis-causing pathogens transmitted?

options.A: Airborne droplets
options.B: Direct skin contact
options.C: Fecal-oral route
options.D: Vector-borne transmission

explanation: Pathogens responsible for gastroenteritis are typically transmitted via the fecal-oral route through contaminated food, water, and poor hygiene practices. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T20#GNS313_U2_T20_h2)

question: How do bacterial enterotoxins primarily cause watery diarrhea in gastroenteritis?

options.A: By completely destroying all intestinal epithelial cells instantly
options.B: By stimulating massive secretion of water and electrolytes into the lumen
options.C: By blocking the absorption of dietary proteins only
options.D: By inducing severe systemic respiratory failure

explanation: Bacterial enterotoxins stimulate the active secretion of water and electrolytes into the intestinal lumen, leading to profuse watery diarrhea without necessarily destroying the mucosal cells. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T20#GNS313_U2_T20_h3)

question: Which factor significantly accelerates transmission dynamics of gastroenteritis in crowded or resource-limited settings?

options.A: High physical activity levels
options.B: Adequate sewage disposal systems
options.C: Contaminated water and poor hand hygiene
options.D: Regular consumption of fruits

explanation: Contaminated water and poor hand hygiene facilitate the fecal-oral spread of pathogens, driving high transmission rates in vulnerable communities. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T20#GNS313_U2_T20_h3)

question: What is considered the most critical immediate threat to monitor during the assessment of a patient with gastroenteritis?

options.A: High-grade fever
options.B: Severe dehydration
options.C: Chronic weight gain
options.D: Hypertension

explanation: Severe dehydration resulting from excessive fluid and electrolyte loss via vomiting and diarrhea is the most critical and life-threatening complication of acute gastroenteritis. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T20#GNS313_U2_T20_h4)

question: Which of the following physical assessment findings indicates significant volume depletion in a child with gastroenteritis?

options.A: Brisk skin turgor and moist lips
options.B: Sunken eyes and decreased urine output
options.C: Bradycardia and flushed skin
options.D: Hyperactive bowel sounds with soft abdomen

explanation: Sunken eyes, lethargy, dry mucous membranes, and decreased or absent urine output are classic clinical signs of dehydration and volume depletion. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T20#GNS313_U2_T20_h4)

question: When are stool microscopy, culture, and sensitivity tests most strongly indicated in gastroenteritis?

options.A: In every mild case of viral vomiting
options.B: When managing suspected bacterial dysentery or persistent diarrhea
options.C: Only after the patient has completely recovered
options.D: To measure the exact blood pressure of the patient

explanation: Stool cultures and sensitivity tests are specifically indicated for persistent diarrhea, suspected bacterial pathogens (such as dysentery with blood), or during outbreaks. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T20#GNS313_U2_T20_h5)

question: What type of acid-base imbalance is commonly associated with severe watery diarrhea due to bicarbonate loss?

options.A: Metabolic alkalosis
options.B: Respiratory alkalosis
options.C: Metabolic acidosis
options.D: Respiratory acidosis

explanation: Loss of bicarbonate-rich intestinal fluids through watery diarrhea frequently leads to metabolic acidosis in gastroenteritis patients. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T20#GNS313_U2_T20_h5)

question: What is the gold standard treatment for mild to moderate dehydration caused by gastroenteritis?

options.A: Intravenous normal saline infusion only
options.B: Oral Rehydration Therapy using ORS
options.C: Strict NPO (nothing by mouth) for 48 hours
options.D: High-dose broad-spectrum antibiotics

explanation: Oral Rehydration Therapy using Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS) is the safe, effective gold standard for treating mild to moderate dehydration by utilizing intestinal sodium-glucose cotransport. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T20#GNS313_U2_T20_h6)

question: Which micronutrient supplementation is recommended by the WHO for children with acute gastroenteritis to reduce diarrhea duration and severity?

options.A: Iron
options.B: Zinc
options.C: Vitamin C
options.D: Calcium

explanation: Zinc supplementation is strongly recommended for children with acute gastroenteritis to shorten the duration and severity of the illness and prevent future episodes. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T20#GNS313_U2_T20_h6)

question: What is the primary cause of hypovolemic shock in a patient with untreated gastroenteritis?

options.A: Severe fluid and electrolyte volume depletion
options.B: Excessive intake of oral antibiotics
options.C: Primary cardiac muscle failure
options.D: Severe allergic reaction to food

explanation: Uncorrected and excessive fluid losses through vomiting and diarrhea lead directly to severe volume depletion, causing hypovolemic shock. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T20#GNS313_U2_T20_h7)

question: Which severe complication involves hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute renal failure, sometimes triggered by specific bacterial strains in gastroenteritis?

options.A: Diabetic ketoacidosis
options.B: Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome
options.C: Appendicitis
options.D: Peptic ulcer disease

explanation: Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS) is a serious complication characterized by hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute renal failure, often associated with specific bacterial enteropathogens. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T20#GNS313_U2_T20_h7)

question: How does exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months help prevent gastroenteritis in infants?

options.A: It exposes the infant to contaminated tap water early.
options.B: It provides passive immunity and reduces diarrheal illness risk.
options.C: It eliminates the need for any future medical checkups.
options.D: It stops the child from eating solid foods permanently.

explanation: Exclusive breastfeeding provides essential antibodies and passive immunity that protect infants against gastrointestinal pathogens and lower the incidence of severe diarrhea. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T20#GNS313_U2_T20_h8)

question: Which public health intervention directly targets the reduction of Rotavirus-associated gastroenteritis hospitalizations in children?

options.A: National immunization programs with Rotavirus vaccines
options.B: Routine administration of anti-malarial prophylaxis
options.C: Mandatory bed net distribution campaigns
options.D: Widespread use of intravenous antibiotics

explanation: Immunization programs featuring the Rotavirus vaccine are specifically designed to prevent severe rotavirus gastroenteritis and decrease hospital admissions in young children. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T20#GNS313_U2_T20_h8)

question: What is another name for Guinea worm disease?

options.A: Schistosomiasis
options.B: Dracunculiasis
options.C: Onchocerciasis
options.D: Lymphatic filariasis

explanation: Guinea worm disease is scientifically known as dracunculiasis, a painful parasitic infection caused by a specific thread-like nematode. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T23#GNS313_U2_T23_h1)

question: Why is Guinea worm disease of particular historical significance in global health?

options.A: It is the most common parasitic infection in urban Nigerian centers.
options.C: It is on the verge of being the second human disease ever eradicated.
options.B: It has a high mortality rate if left untreated with broad-spectrum antibiotics.
options.D: It can be easily transmitted through airborne respiratory droplets.

explanation: Dracunculiasis is a landmark disease because intensive global eradication campaigns have brought it to the brink of complete eradication, following smallpox. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T23#GNS313_U2_T23_h1)

question: What intermediate host is responsible for harboring the third-stage larvae of Dracunculus medinensis?

options.A: Anopheles mosquito
options.B: Blackfly
options.C: Copepod
options.D: Tsetse fly

explanation: Humans contract the disease by swallowing stagnant water that contains copepods, also known as water fleas, which are infected with the larvae. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T23#GNS313_U2_T23_h2)

question: Where do female adult Dracunculus medinensis worms typically migrate within the human body prior to emergence?

options.A: Subcutaneous tissues toward the lower extremities
options.B: The cerebral ventricles and meninges
options.C: The chambers of the human heart
options.D: The upper respiratory airways and bronchi

explanation: Adult female worms migrate through subcutaneous tissues to reach the skin surface, usually on the lower limbs, to facilitate larvae release in water. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T23#GNS313_U2_T23_h2)

question: What is the primary mode of transmission for Guinea worm disease?

options.A: Ingestion of unfiltered, stagnant water containing infected copepods
options.B: Inhalation of airborne droplets from an infected individual coughing
options.C: Direct skin-to-skin contact with an active skin blister
options.D: Bite from an infected vector insect such as a blackfly

explanation: Transmission occurs strictly through drinking stagnant surface water that contains water fleas (copepods) harboring the parasite larvae. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T23#GNS313_U2_T23_h3)

question: Why does an infected individual entering a communal pond perpetuate the transmission cycle?

options.A: It introduces bacterial spores that contaminate the water supply.
options.B: It causes the female worm to release millions of larvae into the water.
options.C: It attracts the vector mosquitoes that carry the parasite to new hosts.
options.D: It releases toxins that poison the copepods and kill local fish populations.

explanation: Contact with water causes the female worm's blister to rupture and expel millions of first-stage larvae into the water source to be eaten by copepods. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T23#GNS313_U2_T23_h3)

question: What is the typical duration of the incubation period for Dracunculus medinensis after ingestion?

options.A: 1 to 2 weeks
options.B: 1 to 2 months
options.C: 10 to 14 months
options.D: 3 to 5 years

explanation: Infected individuals remain asymptomatic during a long incubation period that typically ranges from 10 to 14 months as the worm matures. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T23#GNS313_U2_T23_h4)

question: What local symptom typically prompts an infected individual to immerse their limb in water?

options.A: Numbness and complete loss of sensation in the foot
options.B: Intense burning pain and localized inflammation at the emergence site
options.C: Severe bruising and subcutaneous hemorrhage
options.D: Rapidly spreading necrotic gangrene of the toes

explanation: The emergence of the worm is preceded by an intense, agonizing burning sensation and pain, driving patients to seek relief in water. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T23#GNS313_U2_T23_h4)

question: What is considered the definitive diagnostic sign of Guinea worm disease during a physical examination?

options.A: Elevated white blood cell count in a complete blood count
options.B: Direct visualization of the adult female worm protruding from the skin
options.C: Positive serological antibody test for parasitic nematodes
options.D: Presence of parasite eggs in the patient's stool sample

explanation: The diagnosis is primarily clinical, confirmed definitively by observing the adult female worm emerging from the cutaneous blister or ulcer. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T23#GNS313_U2_T23_h5)

question: Beyond inspecting the skin lesion, what critical action must a nurse take when a suspected case of dracunculiasis is identified?

options.A: Prescribe broad-spectrum oral antiparasitic medications immediately
options.B: Report the case immediately to public health surveillance authorities
options.C: Isolate the patient in a negative-pressure hospital ward
options.D: Administer prophylactic vaccines to all family members

explanation: Immediate reporting to public health authorities is essential for case containment and stopping potential community transmission outbreaks. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T23#GNS313_U2_T23_h5)

question: Why is slow, incremental extraction of the Guinea worm critical during treatment?

options.A: To prevent the worm from laying eggs in the bloodstream
options.B: To prevent the worm from snapping, which causes severe inflammation and infection
options.C: To ensure the worm's head remains attached for surgical suturing
options.D: To allow the patient's body time to produce natural antibodies against the parasite

explanation: If the worm breaks during traction, it retreats into the tissue and causes severe inflammation, pain, and secondary bacterial infection. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T23#GNS313_U2_T23_h6)

question: What preventive medical intervention is routinely given to patients being treated for Guinea worm disease?

options.A: Tetanus toxoid vaccination or booster
options.B: Rabies immunoglobulin injection
options.C: Oral polio vaccine administration
options.D: Intravenous broad-spectrum antimalarial therapy

explanation: Tetanus prophylaxis is routinely administered because skin ulcers caused by emerging worms serve as a portal of entry for tetanus spores. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T23#GNS313_U2_T23_h6)

question: What is the most common secondary complication associated with Guinea worm skin ulcers?

options.A: Secondary bacterial infections such as cellulitis and abscesses
options.B: Systemic viral hepatitis and liver failure
options.C: Pulmonary embolism and respiratory arrest
options.D: Malignant transformation into squamous cell carcinoma

explanation: Breakdown of the skin barrier by the emerging worm frequently leads to secondary bacterial infections like cellulitis and localized abscesses. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T23#GNS313_U2_T23_h7)

question: How can untreated or complicated dracunculiasis affect patients over the long term?

options.A: It can cause permanent blindness and retinal detachment.
options.B: It can lead to permanent joint contractures, physical deformity, and disability.
options.C: It consistently results in permanent chronic kidney disease.
options.D: It frequently causes irreversible neurological paralysis of the upper limbs.

explanation: Severe inflammation and joint involvement can result in permanent joint contractures, muscle wasting, and lifelong physical disability. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T23#GNS313_U2_T23_h7)

question: What is the primary intervention used to prevent the ingestion of Guinea worm larvae in endemic areas without piped water?

options.A: Adding chemical chlorine tablets directly to all swimming rivers
options.B: Filtering all drinking water using fine-mesh cloth or pipe filters
options.C: Boiling all food items before consumption in local markets
options.D: Spraying agricultural fields with specialized insecticides

explanation: Filtering water through fine-mesh cloth or pipe filters effectively strains out infected copepods, preventing ingestion of the parasite larvae. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T23#GNS313_U2_T23_h8)

question: What does active case containment involve in community health nursing practice?

options.A: Quarantining entire villages for up to two years
options.B: Isolating infected individuals to prevent them from contaminating water sources
options.C: Providing immediate surgical removal of the worm under general anesthesia
options.D: Administering prophylactic antibiotics to every resident in the district

explanation: Case containment involves identifying cases early and ensuring infected individuals do not enter water sources, thereby breaking transmission. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T23#GNS313_U2_T23_h8)

question: What is another term commonly used to describe hydatid disease?

options.A: Ascariasis
options.B: Echinococcosis
options.C: Schistosomiasis
options.D: Toxoplasmosis

explanation: Hydatid disease is also known as echinococcosis, caused by the larval stages of Echinococcus tapeworms. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T25#GNS313_U2_T25_h1)

question: Which organs are most commonly affected by the growth of hydatid cysts?

options.A: Liver and lungs
options.B: Kidneys and spleen
options.C: Brain and heart
options.D: Stomach and intestines

explanation: Hydatid cysts most commonly develop in the liver and lungs due to the circulatory pathway of the parasite. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T25#GNS313_U2_T25_h1)

question: Which animals serve as the definitive hosts for the Echinococcus tapeworm?

options.A: Sheep and cattle
options.B: Dogs and foxes
options.C: Pigs and goats
options.D: Humans and rodents

explanation: Carnivorous animals like dogs, wolves, and foxes act as definitive hosts where the adult tapeworm resides in the intestine. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T25#GNS313_U2_T25_h2)

question: How do humans typically become infected with Echinococcus?

options.A: By eating undercooked beef or mutton containing hydatid cysts
options.B: Through the bite of infected mosquitoes
options.C: By ingesting parasite eggs through contaminated food, water, or soil
options.D: By direct skin contact with infected sheep

explanation: Humans become accidental intermediate hosts by ingesting parasite eggs shed in the feces of definitive hosts. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T25#GNS313_U2_T25_h2)

question: What is the primary route of transmission for hydatid disease to humans?

options.A: Inhalation of respiratory droplets
options.B: Fecal-oral ingestion of parasite eggs
options.C: Direct percutaneous penetration
options.D: Vector-borne tick transmission

explanation: Transmission occurs via the fecal-oral route when humans ingest food, water, or soil contaminated with tapeworm eggs. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T25#GNS313_U2_T25_h3)

question: Which demographic group is considered particularly vulnerable to acquiring hydatid disease?

options.A: Children with close contact with dogs
options.B: Urban office workers
options.C: Elderly individuals in non-farming areas
options.D: Deep-sea fishermen

explanation: Children are at higher risk due to their close contact with dogs and poor hand hygiene habits. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T25#GNS313_U2_T25_h3)

question: Which layer of the hydatid cyst is responsible for producing brood capsules and protoscolices?

options.A: The pericyst
options.B: The laminated membrane
options.C: The germinal layer
options.D: The adventitial layer

explanation: The inner germinal layer of the cyst produces brood capsules and protoscolices, which float in the cyst fluid. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T25#GNS313_U2_T25_h4)

question: Why is the liver the most common site for hydatid cyst development?

options.A: It receives the highest concentration of oxygenated blood.
options.B: It acts as the primary filter via the portal venous system after intestinal penetration.
options.C: It secretes bile that attracts the parasite larvae.
options.D: It has a lower body temperature favorable to the parasite.

explanation: Larvae penetrating the intestinal wall enter the portal venous system and are primarily trapped within the hepatic capillary bed. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T25#GNS313_U2_T25_h4)

question: What is a common presentation for a patient with a large hepatic hydatid cyst?

options.A: Right upper quadrant abdominal pain and hepatomegaly
options.B: Severe chronic cough with hemoptysis
options.C: Left lower quadrant pain and bloody stools
options.D: Epigastric burning relieved by food intake

explanation: Large liver cysts cause right upper quadrant pain, an enlarged liver, and sometimes a palpable mass due to mechanical pressure. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T25#GNS313_U2_T25_h5)

question: What severe systemic reaction can occur if a hydatid cyst leaks its fluid into the circulation?

options.A: Septic shock
options.B: Anaphylactic shock
options.C: Cardiogenic shock
options.D: Hypovolemic shock

explanation: Leakage or rupture of cyst fluid can trigger severe allergic manifestations, ranging from urticaria to life-threatening anaphylaxis. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T25#GNS313_U2_T25_h5)

question: Which imaging modality is typically used as the primary tool for diagnosing hepatic hydatid cysts?

options.A: Chest X-ray
options.B: Ultrasonography
options.C: Bone scintigraphy
options.D: Electrocardiography

explanation: Ultrasonography is the primary imaging tool because it is non-invasive, highly sensitive, and can classify liver cysts effectively. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T25#GNS313_U2_T25_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of serological tests like ELISA in suspected hydatid disease?

options.A: To measure liver enzyme levels
options.B: To detect specific anti-Echinococcus antibodies
options.C: To assess kidney function before surgery
options.D: To count white blood cells for bacterial infection

explanation: Serological tests detect specific antibodies against the parasite to help confirm the diagnosis. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T25#GNS313_U2_T25_h6)

question: Which pharmacological agents are primarily used in the medical management of hydatid disease?

options.A: Benzimidazoles like albendazole
options.B: Broad-spectrum penicillins
options.C: Antimalarial artemisinin derivatives
options.D: Antifungal azoles like fluconazole

explanation: Benzimidazoles such as albendazole are the mainstay medical treatment to inhibit parasite metabolism and reduce cyst viability. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T25#GNS313_U2_T25_h7)

question: What does the acronym PAIR stand for in the minimally invasive management of hydatid cysts?

options.A: Palpation, Aspiration, Incision, and Resection
options.B: Puncture, Aspiration, Injection, and Re-aspiration
options.C: Percutaneous Access, Irrigation, and Removal
options.D: Primary Antibiotic Infusion and Resection

explanation: PAIR stands for Puncture, Aspiration, Injection (of scolicidal agent), and Re-aspiration, performed under imaging guidance. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T25#GNS313_U2_T25_h7)

question: What is considered one of the most critical and life-threatening complications of a hydatid cyst?

options.A: Spontaneous or traumatic cyst rupture
options.B: Chronic iron deficiency anemia
options.C: Mild peripheral edema
options.D: Transient hypertension

explanation: Cyst rupture is a major complication that can cause severe anaphylaxis and widespread secondary cyst dissemination. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T25#GNS313_U2_T25_h8)

question: How does the rupture of a hepatic hydatid cyst into the biliary tree typically present clinically?

options.A: Obstructive jaundice and cholangitis
options.B: Severe renal failure
options.C: Acute left-sided heart failure
options.D: Spontaneous bone fractures

explanation: Rupture into the biliary tree obstructs bile flow, leading to jaundice, inflammation (cholangitis), or pancreatitis. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T25#GNS313_U2_T25_h8)

question: What collaborative approach is essential for the effective control and prevention of hydatid disease?

options.A: A One Health approach integrating human, veterinary, and environmental sectors
options.B: Sole reliance on mass human vaccination campaigns
options.C: Strict quarantine of all affected human patients
options.D: Mass culling of all domestic and stray dogs

explanation: A One Health approach integrates human health, veterinary medicine, and environmental measures to successfully disrupt the parasite's life cycle. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T25#GNS313_U2_T25_h9)

question: Which medication is commonly used in veterinary deworming programs to eliminate Echinococcus from dogs?

options.A: Praziquantel
options.B: Albendazole
options.C: Amoxicillin
options.D: Chloroquine

explanation: Praziquantel is the drug of choice for deworming definitive hosts like dogs to clear adult tapeworms from their intestines. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T25#GNS313_U2_T25_h9)

question: What are the predominant Paragonimus species responsible for human infection in West Africa, including Nigeria?

options.A: Paragonimus westermani and Paragonimus kellicotti
options.B: Paragonimus africanus and Paragonimus uterobilateralis
options.C: Schistosoma haematobium and Schistosoma mansoni
options.D: Fasciola hepatica and Clonorchis sinensis

explanation: Paragonimus africanus and Paragonimus uterobilateralis are the specific lung fluke species predominantly found in West Africa and Nigeria. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T26#GNS313_U2_T26_h1)

question: Why is it clinically important for nurses to distinguish paragonimiasis from pulmonary tuberculosis?

options.A: Paragonimiasis is transmitted exclusively via airborne droplets like tuberculosis.
options.B: Misdiagnosis leads to inappropriate anti-tuberculous treatment and delayed care.
options.C: Tuberculosis medications completely cure paragonimiasis within days.
options.D: Paragonimiasis never presents with a cough or hemoptysis.

explanation: Because paragonimiasis mimics tuberculosis, mistaking it leads to ineffective TB drug regimens and prolonged patient suffering. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T26#GNS313_U2_T26_h1)

question: What serves as the first intermediate host in the life cycle of Paragonimus species?

options.A: Freshwater snails
options.B: Freshwater crabs
options.C: Crayfish
options.D: Human beings

explanation: Freshwater snails act as the first intermediate host where miracidia develop through sporocysts and rediae into cercariae. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T26#GNS313_U2_T26_h2)

question: At what stage are Paragonimus larvae infective to the definitive human host?

options.A: Miracidium
options.B: Cercaria
options.C: Metacercaria
options.D: Redia

explanation: Humans acquire the infection by ingesting raw or undercooked crustaceans containing the encysted metacercariae stage. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T26#GNS313_U2_T26_h2)

question: What is the primary mode of transmission of paragonimiasis to humans?

options.A: Inhalation of airborne dust contaminated with parasite eggs
options.B: Ingestion of raw or inadequately cooked freshwater crabs or crayfish
options.C: Swimming or bathing in slow-moving freshwater streams
options.D: Direct skin contact with infected human sputum

explanation: Transmission occurs when humans eat raw or undercooked freshwater crabs and crayfish that harbor the infective metacercariae. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T26#GNS313_U2_T26_h3)

question: Which Nigerian geographic areas are particularly associated with a higher epidemiological risk of paragonimiasis?

options.A: Arid northern semi-desert regions
options.B: Riverine and forested areas like the Niger Delta
options.C: High-altitude urban metropolitan centers
options.D: Dry savannah cattle-rearing communities

explanation: Riverine and forested regions where freshwater crabs are harvested and consumed traditionally have a higher risk of endemic paragonimiasis. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T26#GNS313_U2_T26_h3)

question: What color and characteristic feature typically describes the sputum of a patient with pulmonary paragonimiasis?

options.A: Clear, frothy white sputum without blood
options.B: Rusty, brownish, or blood-stained sputum containing golden-brown eggs
options.C: Bright red, massive hemoptysis with no particulate matter
options.D: Dark green, foul-smelling purulent sputum

explanation: The breakdown of lung tissue and cyst communication with bronchi leads to rusty or blood-stained sputum containing parasite eggs. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T26#GNS313_U2_T26_h4)

question: What is a potential consequence if Paragonimus larvae undergo ectopic migration?

options.A: Development of cerebral lesions leading to seizures and headaches
options.B: Immediate total immunity against future parasitic infections
options.C: Permanent calcification of the entire gastrointestinal tract
options.D: Transformation of the parasite into a tapeworm species

explanation: Ectopic migration into the brain causes cerebral paragonimiasis, presenting with neurological signs like seizures and severe headaches. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T26#GNS313_U2_T26_h4)

question: What is the primary parasitological method used to confirm a diagnosis of pulmonary paragonimiasis?

options.A: Urinalysis for parasite microfilariae
options.B: Sputum microscopy to identify operculated golden-brown eggs
options.C: Lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid culture
options.D: Skin snip test for larval micro-parasites

explanation: Examining sputum under a microscope to find characteristically operculated, golden-brown Paragonimus eggs confirms the diagnosis. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T26#GNS313_U2_T26_h5)

question: Which crucial piece of history should a nurse prioritize when suspecting paragonimiasis?

options.A: History of receiving blood transfusions in urban hospitals
options.B: Dietary consumption of raw or undercooked freshwater crabs and crayfish
options.C: Occupational exposure to industrial chemical fumes
options.D: Family history of congenital heart defects

explanation: A detailed dietary history regarding raw or undercooked freshwater crustaceans is vital to link symptoms to paragonimiasis. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T26#GNS313_U2_T26_h5)

question: What is the primary medication of choice recommended for treating paragonimiasis?

options.A: Albendazole
options.B: Praziquantel
options.C: Metronidazole
options.D: Diethylcarbamazine

explanation: Praziquantel is the frontline drug of choice for eradicating Paragonimus flukes from both pulmonary and ectopic sites. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T26#GNS313_U2_T26_h6)

question: What is a key nursing responsibility when caring for a patient undergoing treatment with Praziquantel for paragonimiasis?

options.A: Instructing the patient to fast completely throughout the duration of therapy
options.B: Monitoring for adverse side effects like dizziness and nausea, and ensuring medication adherence
options.C: Administering the drug via intravenous infusion only in an intensive care setting
options.D: Recommending that the patient consume raw crabs to boost immunity during recovery

explanation: Nurses must monitor for side effects, promote adherence, and offer supportive care to ensure a successful therapeutic outcome. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T26#GNS313_U2_T26_h6)

question: What is a life-threatening complication associated with ectopic migration of Paragonimus to the central nervous system?

options.A: Chronic simple bronchitis
options.B: Cerebral paragonimiasis leading to seizures and intracranial complications
options.C: Permanent blindness due to retinal detachment
options.D: Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome

explanation: Migration of the parasite to the brain causes cerebral paragonimiasis, which can manifest as seizures and severe neurological impairment. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T26#GNS313_U2_T26_h7)

question: How does prompt diagnosis and praziquantel treatment generally affect the prognosis of uncomplicated pulmonary paragonimiasis?

options.A: The prognosis is poor, with inevitable chronic lung failure.
options.B: The prognosis is excellent, resulting in complete resolution of symptoms and lesions.
options.C: The disease becomes dormant and recurs every ten years.
options.D: It permanently alters the patient's blood type.

explanation: Early detection and proper drug therapy yield an excellent prognosis, allowing patients to fully recover without lasting lung damage. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T26#GNS313_U2_T26_h7)

question: What is the most effective behavioral modification that community nurses should promote to prevent paragonimiasis?

options.A: Avoiding all contact with freshwater by wearing heavy winter clothing
options.B: Ensuring all freshwater crabs and crayfish are thoroughly cooked before consumption
options.C: Taking prophylactic anti-tuberculous drugs year-round
options.D: Eliminating all domestic cats and dogs in endemic villages

explanation: Thorough cooking destroys the infective metacercariae present in freshwater crabs and crayfish, effectively preventing transmission. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T26#GNS313_U2_T26_h8)

question: Why is public health nursing education regarding environmental sanitation important in controlling paragonimiasis?

options.A: It prevents the pollution of water bodies with infected human feces and sputum, breaking the life cycle.
options.B: It purifies drinking water to remove heavy metals and industrial wastes.
options.C: It stops freshwater crabs from migrating onto agricultural farmlands.
options.D: It eradicates all species of mosquitoes responsible for malaria transmission.

explanation: Proper sanitation stops parasite eggs from reaching water sources, preventing infection of snails and interrupting the life cycle. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T26#GNS313_U2_T26_h8)

question: To which group of patients should standard precautions be applied?

options.A: Only patients with diagnosed airborne infections
options.B: Only patients presenting with visible bleeding
options.C: All patients regardless of their infectious status
options.D: Only immunocompromised patients in private rooms

explanation: Standard precautions are baseline measures applied to the care of all patients regardless of their diagnosed or presumed infection status. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T9#GNS313_U2_T9_h1)

question: Which of the following body fluids is explicitly excluded from standard precautions unless it contains visible blood?

options.A: Sweat
options.B: Saliva
options.C: Urine
options.D: Semen

explanation: Standard precautions apply to all body fluids, secretions, and excretions except sweat, regardless of whether it contains visible blood. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T9#GNS313_U2_T9_h1)

question: What is the primary purpose of understanding the chain of infection in nursing practice?

options.A: To diagnose the specific strain of a bacterial pathogen
options.B: To interrupt the transmission of infectious agents at various links
options.C: To calculate the financial cost of hospital-acquired infections
options.D: To determine the appropriate dosage of broad-spectrum antibiotics

explanation: Understanding the chain of infection enables nurses to strategically interrupt pathogen transmission at different links to prevent outbreaks. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T9#GNS313_U2_T9_h2)

question: Which of the following best describes an engineering control in infection control?

options.A: Conducting weekly hand hygiene audits for ward staff
options.B: Providing mandatory educational seminars on malaria prevention
options.C: Using safety-engineered sharps disposal containers
options.D: Isolating a patient diagnosed with active pulmonary tuberculosis

explanation: Engineering controls use physical devices, such as safety-engineered sharps containers, to isolate or remove workplace hazards. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T9#GNS313_U2_T9_h2)

question: According to the WHO 'My 5 Moments for Hand Hygiene,' when must a nurse clean their hands?

options.A: Only after completing a full 8-hour shift
options.B: Before touching a patient and before clean/aseptic procedures
options.C: Only when family members request it
options.D: Before entering the hospital administrative office

explanation: The WHO moments include before touching a patient and before clean/aseptic procedures, among other critical instances during care delivery. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T9#GNS313_U2_T9_h3)

question: When is handwashing with soap and water specifically required over alcohol-based hand rubs?

options.A: When hands are visibly soiled or dirty
options.B: Whenever a nurse enters a patient room quickly
options.C: Only at the beginning of a nursing shift
options.D: When the nurse is wearing sterile gloves

explanation: Handwashing with soap and water is mandatory when hands are visibly soiled, dirty, or contaminated with organic matter. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T9#GNS313_U2_T9_h3)

question: What is the typical correct sequence for donning personal protective equipment (PPE)?

options.A: Gloves, gown, mask, eye protection
options.B: Gown, mask or respirator, eye protection, gloves
options.C: Eye protection, gloves, gown, mask
options.D: Mask, gloves, gown, eye protection

explanation: The standard donning sequence starts with the gown, followed by the mask or respirator, eye protection, and gloves last. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T9#GNS313_U2_T9_h4)

question: Which of the following statements regarding medical gloves and hand hygiene is true?

options.A: Gloves eliminate the need for hand hygiene entirely.
options.B: Hand hygiene must be performed immediately after removing gloves.
options.C: Gloves should be washed with soap and water between patients for reuse.
options.D: Alcohol rub can be applied while gloves are still on the hands.

explanation: Gloves do not replace hand hygiene, and hands must always be cleaned immediately after removing gloves to eliminate micro-organisms. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T9#GNS313_U2_T9_h4)

question: What is the recommended action regarding used needles and syringes after an injection?

options.A: Recap the needle immediately using both hands for safety
options.B: Place the uncapped needle and syringe directly into a puncture-resistant safety box
options.C: Break the needle off before throwing it in a standard waste bin
options.D: Store the needle in your pocket until the end of the shift

explanation: Used needles should not be recapped; instead, they must be disposed of uncapped directly into a puncture-resistant safety box. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T9#GNS313_U2_T9_h5)

question: At what capacity should a sharps disposal box be sealed and replaced?

options.A: When it is completely overflowing
options.B: Once every month regardless of fill level
options.C: When it reaches the designated three-quarters fill line
options.D: As soon as the first needle is dropped inside

explanation: Safety boxes should never be overfilled; they must be sealed and replaced when they reach the three-quarters full mark. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T9#GNS313_U2_T9_h5)

question: What should a person do if they do not have a tissue when about to cough or sneeze?

options.A: Cough directly into their bare hands
options.B: Cough into their inner elbow
options.C: Turn around and cough openly into the air
options.D: Cover their mouth with a medical glove and reuse it

explanation: If a tissue is unavailable, coughing or sneezing into the inner elbow prevents hands from becoming contaminated with respiratory droplets. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T9#GNS313_U2_T9_h6)

question: Which type of respiratory protection is required when caring for a patient with suspected pulmonary tuberculosis?

options.A: A standard cloth face covering
options.B: A surgical ear-loop mask
options.C: An N95 or higher-level respirator
options.D: No mask is necessary if standing two meters away

explanation: Airborne pathogens like tuberculosis require high-efficiency respirators such as N95 masks to protect healthcare personnel from inhaling small droplet nuclei. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T9#GNS313_U2_T9_h6)

question: What is the primary objective of cleaning a surface before applying a chemical disinfectant?

options.A: To make the surface smell pleasant for the patient
options.B: To remove visible dirt and organic matter that can deactivate disinfectants
options.C: To polish the furniture to a high shine
options.D: To reduce the drying time of the chemical solution

explanation: Removing organic matter through cleaning is essential because soil and protein can shield microorganisms and neutralize chemical disinfectants. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T9#GNS313_U2_T9_h7)

question: How should environmental surfaces in a hospital ward generally be cleaned to prevent spreading contamination?

options.A: From the dirtiest areas to the cleanest areas
options.B: In a random pattern across the entire room
options.C: From the cleanest areas to the dirtiest areas
options.D: Only when the ward manager inspects the unit

explanation: Cleaning should always progress methodically from the cleanest areas to the dirtiest areas to avoid transferring heavy contamination to clean zones. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T9#GNS313_U2_T9_h7)

question: How should reusable non-critical patient care equipment, such as a blood pressure cuff, be managed between patients?

options.A: It should be stored in the supply room for one week without cleaning.
options.B: It must be cleaned and disinfected between each patient use.
options.C: It only needs to be wiped down at the end of the nursing shift.
options.D: It requires high-level heat sterilization before every application.

explanation: Reusable patient care equipment touching intact skin must be properly cleaned and disinfected between every patient use to prevent cross-infection. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T9#GNS313_U2_T9_h8)

question: What is the correct procedure for handling soiled linen in a hospital ward?

options.A: Shake the linen vigorously to remove dust before bagging
options.B: Rinse the soiled linen in the patient sink immediately
options.C: Place the linen directly into a leak-proof laundry bag with minimum agitation
options.D: Carry the linen openly in your arms to the laundry chute

explanation: Soiled linen should be handled with minimum agitation and placed directly into leak-proof bags at the point of use to prevent spreading pathogens. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T9#GNS313_U2_T9_h8)

question: What is the immediate first-aid action a nurse should take after sustaining a needle-stick injury?

options.A: Squeeze the wound tightly to force out contaminated blood
options.B: Wash the affected skin site immediately with soap and clean water
options.C: Apply an antiseptic alcohol tincture and cover with a tight bandage
options.D: Wait until the end of the shift to report it before cleaning
